title: Sociology
description: Free Sociology study guide: the sociological perspective, research methods, culture and socialization, groups, deviance and stratification, race and gender, family and religion, and social change. 80 practice questions with explanations, 48 flashcards and a practice exam.

units.name: Sociological Perspective

concepts.intro: Sociology studies how society shapes individual lives, and how individuals shape society.
b: C. Wright Mills coined 'the sociological imagination': connecting personal troubles to public issues
One person unemployed is a personal trouble; millions unemployed is a public issue rooted in the economy
Sociologists look for patterns in behavior rather than explaining events only by individual choice
Auguste Comte coined the word 'sociology' and argued society could be studied scientifically (positivism)
Sociology overlaps with psychology, economics and anthropology but focuses on groups and social structure

concepts.intro: Several 19th- and early 20th-century thinkers set the questions sociology still asks.
b: Émile Durkheim: social facts, social solidarity, and his study showing suicide rates vary with social integration
Karl Marx: society is shaped by conflict between classes over the means of production
Max Weber: verstehen (understanding meaning), bureaucracy, and the Protestant ethic's link to capitalism
Harriet Martineau translated Comte and studied social life and women's roles
W. E. B. Du Bois studied race in America and described 'double consciousness'

concepts.intro: Three major lenses ask different questions about the same social fact.
b: Structural functionalism: society is a system of parts that work together to keep stability (Durkheim, Parsons, Merton)
Merton: manifest functions are intended; latent functions are unintended (school also provides childcare)
Conflict theory: society is shaped by inequality and competition for resources (Marx)
Symbolic interactionism: society is built through everyday interaction and shared meanings (Mead, Blumer)
Macro perspectives (functionalism, conflict) study large structures; micro (interactionism) studies face-to-face interaction

keyFacts: Sociological imagination (Mills): link personal troubles to public issues.
Functionalism = stability; conflict theory = inequality; symbolic interactionism = meanings.
Durkheim showed suicide rates vary with social integration.
Manifest functions are intended; latent functions are unintended.
traps: Sociology isn't just 'common sense'. Research often contradicts assumptions.
Conflict theory comes from Marx; functionalism from Durkheim, not the other way around.
Symbolic interactionism is a micro-level perspective.

units.name: Research Methods

concepts.intro: Sociologists use systematic methods to test ideas about society.
b: Steps: choose a topic, review the literature, form a hypothesis, choose a method, collect data, analyze, report
A hypothesis predicts a relationship between an independent variable (cause) and a dependent variable (effect)
Operational definitions state exactly how a concept will be measured
Reliability means consistent measurement; validity means measuring what you intend to measure
Correlation isn't causation: a spurious correlation may be caused by a third variable

concepts.intro: Each method suits different questions.
b: Surveys (questionnaires, interviews) collect data from many people; random samples allow generalization
Experiments test cause and effect by manipulating an independent variable, often in controlled settings
Participant observation and ethnography study groups from the inside over time
Secondary analysis uses existing data such as census records
Quantitative methods use numbers; qualitative methods explore meanings in depth

concepts.intro: Research involving people must protect them.
b: Informed consent: participants must know what they're agreeing to
Confidentiality and anonymity protect participants' identities
Institutional review boards (IRBs) review studies for ethical risks
The Hawthorne effect: people change their behavior when they know they're being studied
Value neutrality (Weber): researchers should keep personal values from distorting findings

keyFacts: Independent variable = cause; dependent variable = effect.
Reliability = consistency; validity = accuracy of measurement.
Hawthorne effect: behavior changes when people know they're observed.
Informed consent is a basic ethical requirement.
traps: A reliable measure can still be invalid (a scale that's consistently 5 lb off).
Correlation alone never proves causation.
Participant observation results usually can't be generalized to a whole population.

units.name: Culture & Socialization

concepts.intro: Culture is the shared beliefs, practices and material objects of a group.
b: Material culture: physical objects (phones, clothing); nonmaterial culture: ideas, values, norms, language
Values are broad ideas about what is good; norms are rules for behavior
Folkways are casual norms; mores are strongly held moral norms; laws are formal norms enforced by the state
Symbols and language let people share meaning; the Sapir–Whorf hypothesis says language shapes thought
Sanctions reward or punish behavior to enforce norms

concepts.intro: Cultures differ widely, and how we judge that difference matters.
b: Ethnocentrism: judging other cultures by the standards of your own
Cultural relativism: understanding a culture on its own terms
Subcultures share distinctive elements within a larger culture; countercultures reject major norms
Culture shock: disorientation when encountering an unfamiliar culture
Cultural diffusion spreads ideas and objects between cultures; cultural lag is when nonmaterial culture trails technology (Ogburn)

concepts.intro: Socialization is the lifelong process of learning the culture and developing a self.
b: Agents of socialization: family, school, peers, mass media, workplace, religion
Cooley's looking-glass self: we see ourselves as we think others see us
Mead: the self develops through play and games, taking the role of the 'generalized other'
Feral and isolated children (e.g. 'Genie') show that social contact is necessary for normal development
Resocialization replaces old norms, often in total institutions like prisons or boot camp (Goffman)

keyFacts: Folkways < mores < laws in seriousness.
Ethnocentrism judges; cultural relativism understands.
Looking-glass self (Cooley): self-image comes from others' reactions.
Total institutions (Goffman) resocialize people.
traps: Values and norms aren't the same: values are ideals, norms are behavior rules.
Cultural relativism doesn't mean approving of every practice. It's a method of understanding.
Subculture vs. counterculture: only a counterculture opposes mainstream norms.

units.name: Social Structure & Groups

concepts.intro: Social structure is the pattern of relationships that organizes a society.
b: Status: a position in society; ascribed statuses are assigned (age, race), achieved statuses are earned (lawyer)
Master status: the status that dominates others in how people are seen
Role: the expected behavior of someone with a status
Role conflict: clashes between different statuses (parent vs. employee); role strain: tension within one status
Goffman's dramaturgy: people manage impressions like actors on a stage (front stage vs. backstage)

concepts.intro: Groups shape identity and behavior.
b: Primary groups are small and intimate (family, close friends); secondary groups are larger and goal-oriented (coworkers)
In-groups command loyalty; out-groups are viewed with competition or hostility
Reference groups set standards we use to evaluate ourselves
Dyads (2 people) are intimate but fragile; triads (3) are more stable but allow coalitions (Simmel)
Groupthink: pressure for agreement leads to poor decisions

concepts.intro: Group pressure and bureaucracy shape how people act.
b: Asch's line experiments: many people conformed to an obviously wrong group answer
Milgram's obedience studies: most participants obeyed an authority figure's orders to give apparent shocks
Weber's ideal bureaucracy: division of labor, hierarchy, written rules, impersonality, merit hiring
The iron law of oligarchy (Michels): organizations tend to be run by a small elite
McDonaldization (Ritzer): efficiency, calculability, predictability and control spreading through society

keyFacts: Ascribed status is assigned; achieved status is earned.
Primary groups are intimate; secondary groups are goal-oriented.
Asch showed conformity; Milgram showed obedience to authority.
Weber's bureaucracy: hierarchy, rules, specialization, impersonality.
traps: Role conflict involves two statuses; role strain involves one status.
Asch studied conformity to peers; Milgram studied obedience to authority.
A master status isn't always achieved. It can be ascribed, like race or disability.

units.name: Deviance & Stratification

concepts.intro: Deviance is behavior that violates norms. Sociologists ask why it happens and who gets labeled.
b: Deviance is relative: what's deviant depends on time, place and group
Durkheim: deviance clarifies norms and can promote social change
Merton's strain theory: deviance results when people lack legitimate means to reach cultural goals (innovation, ritualism, retreatism, rebellion)
Labeling theory (Becker): deviance is a label applied by others; a label can become a self-fulfilling identity
Differential association (Sutherland): deviance is learned from the people we interact with

concepts.intro: Societies use informal and formal controls to enforce norms.
b: Informal social control: disapproval, gossip, praise; formal: police, courts, laws
White-collar crime is committed by high-status people in the course of their jobs (Sutherland)
Conflict theorists note that laws and enforcement often reflect the interests of the powerful
Recidivism is the rate at which released offenders reoffend
Broken windows theory: visible disorder encourages more serious crime (a contested idea)

concepts.intro: Stratification ranks people into layers with unequal access to resources.
b: Weber's three dimensions: class (wealth), status (prestige) and power
Caste systems are closed (status is ascribed); class systems are open (mobility is possible)
Social mobility can be upward, downward, intergenerational or intragenerational
Davis–Moore thesis (functionalist): inequality motivates people to fill important positions
Conflict theorists argue stratification benefits the powerful and reproduces itself across generations

keyFacts: Merton: strain between goals and means produces deviance.
Labeling theory: deviance depends on who gets labeled.
Weber: class, status and power.
Caste = closed system; class = open system.
traps: Deviance isn't the same as crime. Many deviant acts are legal.
Labeling theory focuses on reactions to behavior, not the behavior itself.
The Davis–Moore thesis is functionalist; conflict theorists criticize it.

units.name: Race, Gender & Inequality

concepts.intro: Race and ethnicity are social categories with real consequences.
b: Race is socially constructed: categories based on perceived physical traits that vary across societies and time
Ethnicity refers to shared culture, ancestry, language or religion
Prejudice is an attitude; discrimination is an action
Institutional (systemic) discrimination is built into policies and practices, like historical redlining in housing
Patterns of intergroup relations include assimilation, pluralism, segregation and genocide

concepts.intro: Gender is the set of social expectations attached to being male or female.
b: Sex refers to biological characteristics; gender refers to socially learned roles and identities
Gender socialization begins early through toys, clothing, media and expectations
The gender pay gap persists partly because of occupational segregation and caregiving expectations
The 'glass ceiling' describes invisible barriers to advancement
Feminist theory examines how gender inequality is created and maintained

concepts.intro: Inequalities overlap and combine.
b: Intersectionality (Kimberlé Crenshaw) examines how race, class, gender and other identities combine to shape experience
A minority group is defined by less power, not by smaller numbers
Stereotypes are oversimplified generalizations about a group
Scapegoating blames a less powerful group for problems
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 outlawed many forms of discrimination in the U.S.

keyFacts: Race is socially constructed; ethnicity is shared culture.
Prejudice = attitude; discrimination = action.
Institutional discrimination is built into policies and systems.
Intersectionality: identities overlap to shape inequality.
traps: A minority group isn't necessarily a numerical minority. It's about power.
Discrimination can happen without individual prejudice, through institutions.
Sex (biological) and gender (social) aren't the same concept.

units.name: Family & Religion

concepts.intro: Family forms vary widely across cultures and have changed over time.
b: Nuclear family: parents and children; extended family: several generations or relatives
Monogamy is marriage to one person; polygamy to several (polygyny: one husband, several wives)
Patrilineal, matrilineal and bilateral descent trace kinship differently
Trends in the U.S.: later marriage, more cohabitation, more single-parent and blended families
Endogamy: marrying within a group; exogamy: marrying outside it

concepts.intro: Each theoretical lens highlights different family functions and problems.
b: Functionalists: families socialize children, regulate sexuality, provide economic and emotional support
Conflict theorists: families can reproduce inequality in wealth and gendered power
Symbolic interactionists: family members create meaning through daily interaction
The 'second shift' (Hochschild): working women often do most housework after paid work
Family violence and divorce are studied as social patterns, not just private troubles

concepts.intro: Religion is a system of beliefs and practices about the sacred.
b: Durkheim distinguished the sacred (set apart, awe-inspiring) from the profane (ordinary)
Functions of religion: meaning, social cohesion, social control, support in crisis
Marx called religion 'the opium of the people,' arguing it distracts from inequality
Weber linked the Protestant ethic to the rise of capitalism
Secularization is the declining influence of religion in public life; fundamentalism resists it

keyFacts: Nuclear family = parents and children; extended = multiple generations.
Durkheim: sacred vs. profane.
Marx: religion as 'opium of the people'.
Weber: Protestant ethic and the spirit of capitalism.
traps: Polygamy is the general term; polygyny is specifically one husband with several wives.
Secularization doesn't mean religion disappears. It means its public influence declines.
Durkheim's 'profane' means ordinary, not offensive.

units.name: Social Change & Movements

concepts.intro: Societies change through technology, population, environment, ideas and conflict.
b: Technology (the printing press, the internet) reshapes work, communication and relationships
Demographic change: population growth, aging, migration and urbanization
Cultural diffusion spreads ideas across societies
Modernization: the shift from traditional, small-scale societies to industrial, urban ones
Tönnies contrasted Gemeinschaft (close community) with Gesellschaft (impersonal society)

concepts.intro: Not all group behavior is organized or planned.
b: Crowds, mobs, riots, panics, fads and fashions are forms of collective behavior
Contagion theory: crowds make people act irrationally (Le Bon)
Convergence theory: like-minded people come together, so crowds reflect members' existing views
Emergent-norm theory: crowds develop new norms as a situation unfolds
Rumors and moral panics spread quickly, especially through media

concepts.intro: Social movements are organized efforts to promote or resist change.
b: Types: reform (change some aspects), revolutionary (overturn the system), resistance (block change), alternative (change individuals)
Resource mobilization theory: success depends on money, members, leaders and organization
Relative deprivation: people mobilize when they feel worse off than others or than expected
Life cycle: emergence, coalescence, bureaucratization, decline
Examples: the Civil Rights Movement, the women's suffrage movement, environmental movements

keyFacts: Gemeinschaft = close community; Gesellschaft = impersonal society.
Contagion, convergence and emergent-norm theories explain crowd behavior.
Resource mobilization: movements need resources and organization.
Relative deprivation drives mobilization more than absolute poverty.
traps: Relative deprivation is about perceived gaps, not absolute poverty.
Reform movements seek partial change; revolutionary movements seek total change.
Convergence theory says crowds reflect members' existing views. It isn't about contagion.

quiz.q: The sociological imagination, as described by C. Wright Mills, is the ability to:
o: Connect personal experiences to larger social forces
quiz.e: Mills contrasted private 'troubles' with public 'issues'.

quiz.q: Who coined the term 'sociology'?
quiz.e: Comte argued society could be studied with scientific methods.

quiz.q: Durkheim's study of suicide showed that suicide rates:
o: Vary with how integrated people are in society
Are the same in every society
quiz.e: Social integration and regulation affected rates across groups.

quiz.q: Which perspective views society as a system of parts working to maintain stability?
quiz.e: Functionalists ask what purpose a social institution serves.

quiz.q: A sociologist studying how the wealthy use schools to keep advantages is using:
quiz.e: Conflict theory focuses on inequality and power.

quiz.q: A researcher studying how people use greetings to signal status is taking which approach?
quiz.e: It focuses on everyday interaction and meaning.

quiz.q: An unintended consequence of an institution, like college helping students find spouses, is a:
quiz.e: Merton called intended purposes manifest and unintended ones latent.

quiz.q: Max Weber's concept of verstehen means:
o: Understanding the meaning people give their actions
quiz.e: Weber stressed interpreting social action from actors' perspective.

quiz.q: W. E. B. Du Bois described 'double consciousness' as:
o: Seeing oneself through one's own eyes and through a racist society's eyes
quiz.e: He wrote about African Americans' experience in The Souls of Black Folk.

quiz.q: Which is a macro-level perspective?
quiz.e: Conflict theory analyzes large-scale structures and inequality.

quiz.q: In a study of whether education level affects income, education is the:
quiz.e: Education is the presumed cause.

quiz.q: A measure that gives the same results each time is:
quiz.e: Reliability means consistency.

quiz.q: A survey that claims to measure happiness but really measures income lacks:
quiz.e: Validity is whether you measure what you intend to.

quiz.q: Workers became more productive simply because they knew they were being studied. This is the:
quiz.e: Named for studies at the Hawthorne Works factory.

quiz.q: A researcher joins a motorcycle club for a year to study its culture. This is:
quiz.e: The researcher studies the group from within.

quiz.q: Using census data collected by the government is an example of:
quiz.e: It uses data someone else already gathered.

quiz.q: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together because both increase in summer. This is a:
quiz.e: A third variable (hot weather) drives both.

quiz.q: Which is a basic ethical rule for research with human subjects?
quiz.e: Participants must understand and agree to take part.

quiz.q: Which method best establishes cause and effect?
quiz.e: Manipulating the independent variable while controlling others supports causal claims.

quiz.q: Research that explores the meanings people give their experiences through interviews is:
quiz.e: Qualitative research focuses on in-depth understanding.

quiz.q: Which is an example of nonmaterial culture?
o: A national flag as a physical object
quiz.e: Beliefs and values are nonmaterial.

quiz.q: Wearing pajamas to a job interview violates a:
quiz.e: It's a casual custom, not a serious moral rule.

quiz.q: Norms whose violation provokes strong moral outrage are:
quiz.e: Mores concern core moral standards.

quiz.q: Judging another culture's food as 'disgusting' because it differs from yours shows:
quiz.e: It uses your culture as the standard.

quiz.q: A group that rejects mainstream norms, such as a radical commune, is a:
quiz.e: Countercultures actively oppose dominant values.

quiz.q: Laws about online privacy lagging behind smartphone technology is an example of:
quiz.e: Ogburn: nonmaterial culture adjusts more slowly than technology.

quiz.q: Cooley's 'looking-glass self' means:
o: We copy what we see in mirrors
We develop self-image from how we think others see us
quiz.e: Others act as a mirror for our sense of self.

quiz.q: Which is a primary agent of socialization in early childhood?
quiz.e: Family shapes language, values and identity first.

quiz.q: Boot camp stripping recruits of old identities is an example of:
quiz.e: Total institutions rebuild identity around new norms.

quiz.q: Cases of severely isolated children show that:
o: Social interaction is essential for normal development
quiz.e: Isolated children had serious delays in language and social skills.

quiz.q: Being a teenager is an example of a(n):
quiz.e: Age is assigned, not earned.

quiz.q: Being a doctor is an example of a(n):
quiz.e: It is earned through training.

quiz.q: A student-athlete torn between practice and a group project is experiencing:
quiz.e: Two different statuses make competing demands.

quiz.q: A teacher who struggles to be both friendly and a strict grader experiences:
quiz.e: The tension is within a single status.

quiz.q: Your family is an example of a:
quiz.e: Primary groups are small, intimate and long-lasting.

quiz.q: Most subjects in Asch's experiment conformed at least once to a wrong answer. This shows:
o: Group pressure can override individual judgment
quiz.e: About three-quarters conformed at least once.

quiz.q: Milgram's experiments demonstrated:
quiz.e: Many participants continued giving apparent shocks when instructed.

quiz.q: Which is a feature of Weber's ideal bureaucracy?
o: Written rules and a hierarchy of authority
quiz.e: Bureaucracy relies on rules, hierarchy and impersonality.

quiz.q: Goffman's 'front stage' refers to:
o: How people act when performing for an audience
quiz.e: Dramaturgy compares social life to a performance.

quiz.q: A group of advisers who ignore doubts to maintain agreement shows:
quiz.e: Pressure for consensus can lead to poor decisions.

quiz.q: Durkheim argued that deviance:
o: Clarifies norms and can promote change
quiz.e: Punishing deviance reaffirms shared norms.

quiz.q: In Merton's strain theory, a student who cheats to get good grades (accepting the goal but not the legitimate means) is an:
quiz.e: Innovation accepts goals but uses illegitimate means.

quiz.q: Labeling theory argues that:
o: Everyone is equally likely to be labeled
Deviance depends on how others react to behavior
quiz.e: Becker: deviant behavior is behavior people so label.

quiz.q: Differential association theory says deviance is:
quiz.e: Sutherland: we learn attitudes toward crime from our associates.

quiz.q: Embezzlement by a corporate executive is an example of:
quiz.e: Sutherland described crimes committed by high-status people in their occupations.

quiz.q: Weber's three dimensions of stratification are:
quiz.e: He separated economic position, prestige and political power.

quiz.q: A system in which status is fixed at birth and mobility is nearly impossible is a:
quiz.e: Caste systems are closed.

quiz.q: A child of factory workers becoming a surgeon is an example of:
quiz.e: The change is across generations and upward.

quiz.q: The Davis–Moore thesis claims inequality:
o: Motivates talented people to fill important jobs
quiz.e: It is a functionalist explanation of stratification.

quiz.q: Gossip and disapproving looks are forms of:
quiz.e: They enforce norms without official authority.

quiz.q: Saying race is 'socially constructed' means:
o: Racial categories are created by societies and change over time
Race has no real effects on people's lives
Everyone belongs to the same race
quiz.e: Categories vary by place and era, yet they have real consequences.

quiz.q: Prejudice differs from discrimination because prejudice is:
o: An attitude, while discrimination is an action
quiz.e: You can hold prejudice without acting on it, and vice versa.

quiz.q: Bank policies that historically denied loans in certain neighborhoods are an example of:
quiz.e: Redlining was built into lending practices.

quiz.q: A society where different groups keep their cultures while coexisting equally practices:
quiz.e: Pluralism values diversity within one society.

quiz.q: Gender, as distinct from sex, refers to:
quiz.e: Gender is shaped by culture and socialization.

quiz.q: The 'glass ceiling' describes:
o: Invisible barriers to advancement for women and minorities
quiz.e: People can see the top positions but face unwritten obstacles.

quiz.q: Intersectionality is the idea that:
o: Race, class, gender and other identities combine to shape experiences of inequality
Gender is the only important identity
quiz.e: Crenshaw introduced the term.

quiz.q: In sociology, a minority group is defined mainly by:
o: Being less than half the population
Having less power and facing unequal treatment
quiz.e: Numerical size doesn't define minority status.

quiz.q: Blaming an economic crisis on immigrants is an example of:
quiz.e: A less powerful group is blamed for broader problems.

quiz.q: Which U.S. law outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin?
quiz.e: It banned discrimination in employment and public accommodations.

quiz.q: A household with grandparents, parents and children is a(n):
quiz.e: It includes more than two generations.

quiz.q: Polygyny is:
o: One wife with more than one husband
One husband with more than one wife
quiz.e: Polyandry is the reverse.

quiz.q: Marrying someone from your own social group is:
quiz.e: Endo- means within.

quiz.q: From a functionalist view, a key function of the family is to:
quiz.e: Functionalists emphasize contributions to stability.

quiz.q: Hochschild's 'second shift' refers to:
o: Housework that working women often do after their paid jobs
quiz.e: It highlights unequal division of household labor.

quiz.q: Durkheim's 'sacred' refers to:
o: Things set apart and inspiring awe
quiz.e: The profane is the ordinary.

quiz.q: Marx described religion as:
quiz.e: He saw it as dulling awareness of exploitation.

quiz.q: Weber argued that the Protestant ethic:
o: Encouraged hard work and saving that supported capitalism
quiz.e: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905).

quiz.q: Secularization refers to:
o: The declining influence of religion in public life
quiz.e: Religion becomes more private, with less public authority.

quiz.q: A family formed when divorced parents remarry and combine children is a:
quiz.e: It combines children from previous relationships.

quiz.q: Tönnies' Gemeinschaft describes:
o: Close-knit community based on tradition and personal ties
quiz.e: Gesellschaft is the impersonal, modern contrast.

quiz.q: A sudden craze for a toy that fades within months is a:
quiz.e: Fads are short-lived collective enthusiasms.

quiz.q: Contagion theory argues that crowds:
o: Cause people to act irrationally as emotions spread
quiz.e: Le Bon described the 'group mind'.

quiz.q: Emergent-norm theory says crowd behavior:
o: Follows new norms that develop during the event
quiz.e: Norms emerge as people interpret the situation.

quiz.q: A movement seeking to change specific laws without overturning the system is a:
quiz.e: Reform movements aim at partial change.

quiz.q: Resource mobilization theory explains movement success by:
o: Access to money, members and organization
quiz.e: Grievances alone aren't enough without resources.

quiz.q: People who protest because their wages lag behind others' are motivated by:
quiz.e: They compare themselves to others or to expectations.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a resistance movement?
o: A group organizing to stop a proposed policy change
A movement to overthrow the government
quiz.e: Resistance movements try to block change.

quiz.q: Rapid growth of cities as people move from rural areas is called:
quiz.e: Urbanization is a major source of social change.

quiz.q: The stage when a movement becomes formally organized with paid staff is:
quiz.e: Bureaucratization comes after the movement coalesces.

PART_A.q: Explaining high unemployment by pointing to the closure of a region's factories rather than individual laziness uses:
PART_A.e: It connects personal troubles to public issues.

PART_A.q: A study finds that people who own more books score higher on reading tests. Why can't we conclude books cause higher scores?
o: The sample must be too small
A third variable, such as family income, may explain both
PART_A.e: Correlation isn't causation; confounders may be involved.

PART_A.q: Learning how to behave in a new job before you start it is called:
PART_A.e: People practice future roles in advance.

PART_A.q: Which is an example of a secondary group?
PART_A.e: Secondary groups are larger, impersonal and goal-oriented.

PART_A.q: According to labeling theory, why might two teens who commit the same act end up with different futures?
o: Only one may be officially labeled deviant and treated that way
PART_A.e: Labels shape how others treat people and how they see themselves.

PART_A.q: Which is the clearest example of institutional discrimination?
o: One person telling a racist joke
A private dislike of a group
Standardized requirements that systematically exclude a group without explicit intent
PART_A.e: Discrimination can operate through policies, not just individual attitudes.

PART_A.q: A functionalist would most likely emphasize that religion:
o: Builds social cohesion and shared values
Is created in everyday interaction only

PART_B2.q: Explain how two different agents of socialization might teach a child conflicting norms.
PART_B2.sa: Name two agents and a specific conflict. For example, family may teach modesty and obedience to elders while peer groups reward rebellion and status-seeking; or school teaches cooperation while media glorifies individual fame. The child must choose between norms or blend them, which shows socialization is shaped by several sources.

PART_B2.q: Compare functionalist and conflict explanations of social stratification.
PART_B2.sa: Functionalists (Davis–Moore) argue that inequality motivates talented people to train for important jobs by offering greater rewards, so stratification benefits society. Conflict theorists argue that the powerful use their advantages (wealth, networks, education) to pass privilege to their children, so stratification preserves inequality rather than rewarding merit. A strong answer uses an example such as unequal school funding.

PART_C.q: Choose a social issue (e.g. homelessness, school dropout, obesity) and analyze it using all three major sociological perspectives.
PART_C.sa: A strong answer names the issue and applies each perspective correctly. Functionalist: how the issue relates to institutions failing to perform functions, or the latent functions it serves. Conflict: how inequality in resources and power creates or sustains it and who benefits. Symbolic interactionist: how labels, meanings and interactions shape experiences (e.g. stigma of being labeled 'homeless'). It ends with which perspective explains the most, with evidence.

PART_C.q: Design a study to test whether after-school jobs affect high school students' grades. Describe your method, variables, sample and one ethical concern.
PART_C.sa: Independent variable: hours worked per week; dependent variable: GPA (operationally defined as school-reported GPA). A survey of a random sample of students across several schools with confidentiality protections, or a longitudinal design comparing grades before and after starting work. Control for confounders like family income. Ethical concerns: informed consent (including parental consent for minors) and protecting grade data. Correlational findings can't prove causation.
